Use this page when your study is a nested case-control study inside the
register population. It comes after [Build your study
population](build-study-population.qmd), and it reuses the person table built
on [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd), so you need Steps 1 and 2 there
even though you will not match a comparison cohort. The group you identified is
here your cases (those who developed the outcome), and their index date is the
outcome date. For each case you sample controls: people without the outcome who
were at risk exactly when the case had the outcome. When you are done you have a
matched dataset of cases and controls with a matched-set id.

Case-control is especially efficient when the outcome is rare, or when a
covariate is expensive to extract for the whole cohort. The design choice
between cohort and case-control is in [Phase 1 - what type of
study](plan-your-study.qmd#study-type).

::: {.callout-warning title="Structural guidance, not verified code"}
The examples show the shape of each step. They have **not yet been run end to end
on real register data**, so treat them as a starting point: check the column names
against your own delivery, and check the logic against your analysis plan.
Confirm too that `heaven::incidenceMatch()` and `Epi::ccwc()` are available on
your project.
:::

<details>
<summary>Classic case-control vs. nested case-control: what is the difference?</summary>

- **Classic case-control:** you find cases (with the outcome) and select controls (without the outcome) from the population, often without a defined cohort with follow-up behind it. Exposure is typically ascertained retrospectively (e.g. interview) - vulnerable to recall and selection bias, and choosing controls is hard.
- **Nested case-control:** the case-control study sits inside a defined cohort (e.g. a registry cohort followed over time). Cases are those who develop the outcome during follow-up; controls are sampled from those who were at risk (outcome-free) exactly when the case had the outcome (risk-set / incidence-density sampling). Exposure comes from registry data collected *before* the outcome → less recall bias.

In register research at DST you almost always do the nested variant: the cohort already exists in the registers. Advantages: exposure is measured beforehand, and the odds ratio from incidence-density sampling estimates the rate/hazard ratio without a rare-outcome assumption. That is what this page shows.

</details>

## The principle: incidence-density sampling

Controls are selected by risk-set (incidence-density) sampling: for each
case you draw controls who, on the case's index date (= the outcome date), (1)
have not yet developed the outcome and (2) meet the inclusion criteria. A person
can be a control for one case and later become a case themselves. That is
correct in this design: excluding people who later become cases from the
controls biases the estimate ([Lubin & Gail
1984](https://doi.org/10.2307/2530744)).

It is the same mechanic as the matching in [Comparison
cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd) - only the "event" has changed: here it is
the outcome (case), not an exposure. So this page also reuses the person table
from there.

## Step 1 - Build the dataset for matching {.step-heading}

Identifying cases and excluding prevalent cases are done on [Build your study
population](build-study-population.qmd). Here you need one row per person and residence spell, with matching variables and the dates eligibility
depends on. Reuse the `pool` from [Comparison cohort, Step
2](comparison-cohort.qmd#step-2---build-the-comparison-pool) (demographics +
death date + first outcome date), and `demographics` and the migration events
`vnds_ev` from Step 1 there, for the residence spells. For case-control, though:

- **Exposure is not an eligibility criterion here:** unlike the comparison
  cohort, where a control must be exposure-free at index. In case-control,
  exposure is what you study: you measure it for both cases and
  controls afterwards and do not use it to decide who can be a control. A
  control just needs to be outcome-free (and meet your other criteria) at the
  case's index.
- **Who is a case, and when:** the outcome date is the index date.

```r
# Step 1: build the dataset for matching ---------------------------------------
# 'pool' = one row per person from Comparison cohort, Step 2 (pnr, foed_dag, sex, birth_year,
#          death_date, first_outcome_date); 'vnds_ev' = all migration events and
#          'demographics' = one row per person, both from Comparison cohort, Step 1.
#          The exposure date in 'pool' is NOT used here.
STUDY_END <- as.Date("2022-12-31")                # we choose: last day of the study

# Residence spells, as in Comparison cohort, Route A: one row per period of residence,
# from birth or an immigration to the next migration event (NA = no later event).
# incidenceMatch() allows only one at-risk interval per row, so a person who left and
# came back gets one row per spell. join_by(closest()) needs dplyr 1.1.0 or newer.
spells <- bind_rows(
  demographics %>% select(pnr, spell_start = foed_dag),                            # from birth
  vnds_ev %>% filter(indud_kode == "I") %>% select(pnr, spell_start = haend_dato)  # from each immigration
) %>%
  left_join(vnds_ev %>% select(pnr, spell_end = haend_dato),
            join_by(pnr, closest(spell_start < spell_end)))   # the next migration event after the start

all_persons <- pool %>%
  inner_join(spells, by = "pnr", relationship = "one-to-many") %>%
  transmute(                                       # keep ONLY the columns we name
    spell_id   = paste(pnr, spell_start),          # one id per row (incidenceMatch needs a unique id)
    pnr,
    # 1 = case: the outcome falls within the study period AND within this spell (resident
    # when it happened); 0 = potential control. An outcome after STUDY_END is NOT a case.
    case       = if_else(!is.na(first_outcome_date) & first_outcome_date <= STUDY_END &
                           spell_start <= first_outcome_date &
                           (is.na(spell_end) | spell_end > first_outcome_date), 1L, 0L),
    sex        = as.factor(sex),                   # matching variable MUST be factor/character
    birth_year = as.factor(birth_year),            # matching variable
    case_index = if_else(case == 1L, first_outcome_date, as.Date(NA)),  # the case index = outcome date (NA if not a case)
    # Entry = the date the person first meets the inclusion criteria within this spell:
    # here age >= 18 and 5 years continuous residence - adapt
    entry      = pmax(foed_dag + ceiling(18 * 365.25),     # age >= 18
                      spell_start + ceiling(5 * 365.25)),  # 5 years residence in this spell
    # end_fu = when this row leaves the risk set: the EARLIEST of the next migration event
    #          (end of the spell), death, own outcome (they become a case then) or study end.
    end_fu     = pmin(spell_end, death_date, first_outcome_date, STUDY_END, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  filter(entry < end_fu)                           # never at risk in this spell (e.g. outcome before entry) -> neither case nor control
```

## Step 2 - Sample controls {.step-heading}

Two routes. Both do incidence-density sampling; pick one.

**Route A: `heaven::incidenceMatch()`.** The sibling of `exposureMatch()` from
[Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd), but the "event" is the outcome.

```r
# Step 2 (Route A): sample with incidenceMatch() -------------------------------
library(heaven)   # incidenceMatch

# Argument (left of =) <- value we set (usually a column name in quotes)
matched <- incidenceMatch(
  ptid         = "spell_id",             # the row-id column (one row per person and residence spell)
  event        = "case",                 # the column that is 1 for case (outcome), 0 for potential control
  terms        = c("sex", "birth_year"), # matching variables (exact match; factor/character)
  data         = all_persons,            # the dataset from Step 1
  n.controls   = 5,                      # controls per case
  case.index   = "case_index",           # the case's index date (the outcome date)
  end.followup = "end_fu",               # when a person stops being eligible as a control
  date.terms   = "entry",                # a control must have entered before the case's index
  seed         = 20260620                # reproducibility
)
# Output: data.table with 'case.id' identifying each matched set (1 case + its controls)
# dplyr functions work on it as it is; as_tibble(matched) turns it into a tibble
```

**Route B: `Epi::ccwc()`.** Simple risk-set sampling from entry and
exit times; not counter-matching). Confirm arguments with `?Epi::ccwc`.

<details>
<summary>Route B code: sample with Epi::ccwc() instead of heaven</summary>

```r
# Step 2 (Route B): sample with Epi::ccwc() ------------------------------------
library(Epi)   # ccwc - case-control within cohort

cohort <- all_persons %>%
  mutate(
    entry = entry,                                # each row's own entry date (from Step 1)
    exit  = end_fu,                               # exit time = end of risk time (from Step 1)
    fail  = case                                  # 1 if the person is a case at exit (0 if outcome after STUDY_END)
  )

ncc <- ccwc(
  entry    = entry, exit = exit, fail = fail,     # entry time, exit time, failure at exit
  controls = 5,                                   # controls per case
  match    = list(sex, birth_year),               # matching variables
  include  = list(pnr),                           # keep pnr in the output
  data     = cohort
)
# Output: the matched-set id is called 'Set' here (not 'case.id') and the case
# indicator 'Fail' (1 = case, 0 = control)
```

</details>

::: {.callout-note}
**Same rules as in [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd):** apply
inclusion and exclusion criteria before sampling and to everyone (cases and
pool), and set a `seed`. A control can be drawn for several cases, and a person
can be a control before becoming a case; both follow from sampling from the risk
set, so do not remove them. `incidenceMatch()` itself handles the risk-set time dimension via
`case.index` + `end.followup`.
:::

## Analysis: conditional logistic regression

The analysis itself belongs to [Regression](regression.qmd) (Phase 13);
here only briefly, so you know where this leads. Matched case-control data
can be analysed with conditional logistic regression
(`survival::clogit()` with a `strata()` term per matched set), so the matching
is respected; the odds ratio from an incidence-density design estimates the
rate/hazard ratio. This is the standard approach for matched case-control
studies. Before the analysis you attach exposure and covariates to the matched
persons (from [Phase 11](extract-variables.qmd)/[Phase
12](data-manipulation.qmd)). Measure exposure in a window defined relative to
each matched set's index date (the case's outcome date), the same window for
the case and its controls. The matched-set id is called `case.id` (Route A) or
`Set` (Route B).

## Next step: extract exposure and covariates {#what-now}

You have a matched dataset (cases + controls) with a matched-set id (`case.id`
or `Set`). Use `pnr` to extract exposure and covariates for everyone in the
dataset:

```r
cc_pnrs <- unique(matched$pnr) # all pnr's (cases + controls) for the other extractions
```

  | Extraction                         | Phase                                |
  | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
  | Exposure + covariates              | [Phase 11](extract-variables.qmd) |
  | Comorbidity                        | [Comorbidity](comorbidity.qmd)       |
  | Assemble into one analysis dataset | [Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd) |
  | Conditional logistic regression    | [Phase 13](analysis.qmd)          |
